seo.title: Karmic tail 15 5 8 compatibility: meaning for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 15 5 8 compatibility: the Devil at the entry, the Hierophant in the middle, Justice as the main task, told through Jacob, Rachel and Laban.

title: Karmic tail 15-5-8 in compatibility: seven years for Rachel and the heap of witness
short: In late Victorian England, lovers about to part gave each other rings and brooches bearing a single word: Mizpah. Beside it they engraved a verse from Genesis: "The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another." Fashion turned these words into a vow of faithfulness across distance. Who first spoke them, and to whom, was never engraved on the brooches.

sections.h2: How a couple gets the tail 15-5-8
paragraphs: A couple's matrix is not calculated from one date. Each of its points is the sum of the matching points of two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is greater than 22, its digits are added together. The couple's tail is three such sums: the entry to the task M, the middle N and the main task D.
Example: a couple born on 09.05.1976 and 05.07.1975. The first partner's personal tail is 3-22-19, the second partner's is 12-19-7. The points are added in pairs:

The middle of a couple's tail is not recalculated from the two outer numbers: the five here is the sum of the middles of the two personal tails, 22 and 19. For the tail 15-5-8 it happens to match the sum of the ends anyway: 15 + 8 = 23 → 5. That is why the same order also occurs as one person's personal tail, for 4,275 dates since 1900. It is a different calculation with different roles for the points; the personal tail has its own article, and its conclusions do not carry over to the couple.

No other order of these numbers occurs for a couple. The first number of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, and of 15, 5 and 8 only 15 is. The tail itself occurs in roughly one couple in 96 (1.043%), 35th place among the 97 possible couple tails. For the couple in the example, the centre is 11 + 5 = 16, The Tower, and the couple's values are 21, The World. The investigation will come back to both numbers.

sections.h2: First clue: neither partner brings the Devil
paragraphs: Everyone has an entry to their personal tail, and in couples with the tail 15-5-8 only two combinations meet at these entries. In 78% of couples one partner has The Hanged Man (12) there and the other The Empress (3). In the rest it is The Lovers (6) and The Hermit (9). Neither partner has 15 there, and neither can: the sum has to come to exactly 15. **The Devil of this tail does not live in either partner alone. It appears only between them.**

In Jacob's story this is visible from the first scene, if it is read through the cards (the reading is ours). Jacob on his own is a man of service and waiting: The Hanged Man, whose list in Waite includes "trials, sacrifice". Rachel on her own is the shepherdess of her father's flocks, of whom the text says she "was beautiful and well favoured" (Genesis 29:17). Abundance and beauty belong to The Empress. Apart, there is nothing dark in either of them. But the moment they meet, a bargain appears: "I will serve thee seven years for Rachel" (Genesis 29:18). That is how Genesis casts the roles; in a living couple either partner may turn out to be The Hanged Man or The Empress, and gender decides nothing here.

Waite's divinatory list for The Devil includes "vehemence" and "extraordinary efforts". A stone lay over the well that the shepherds rolled away only all together: "We cannot, until all the flocks be gathered together" (Genesis 29:8). Jacob saw Rachel and rolled it away alone. Then he kissed her, "lifted up his voice, and wept". And the seven years of service "seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her" (Genesis 29:20). That is how this entry works: desire compresses time and moves stones.

In the sixteenth century the Portuguese poet Camões wrote a sonnet about this, one of the best known in his language. It has a line that names the hook more precisely than any commentary: Jacob served "not the father, he served her, and her alone he sought as his reward" (our translation). Reward: this is where the Devil hides inside love. The term runs out, and Jacob says to Laban: "Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled" (Genesis 29:21). That is how people speak of wages at the end of a contract.

For Lisovskaya, the couple's entry to the task is what the two want together: their shared wishes and their "common language". The point stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can turn into resistance. For a 15-5-8 couple, the common language at the entry is the language of price. "I moved cities for us." "I waited three years for a decision." "I left my job so we could be together." The desire is real, and so is the price. But a price paid in silence turns into an IOU, and one day it is presented for payment. Lisovskaya sums up the fifteenth energy in a couple in one thought: nobody belongs to anybody.

sections.h2: Second clue: "it must not be so done in our country"
paragraphs: Jacob gets his wedding by all the rules: "Laban gathered together all the men of the place, and made a feast" (Genesis 29:22). The midrash Genesis Rabbah (70:19) tells what it looked like from the inside. Laban took a pledge from the neighbours that no one would give the secret away, and with those pledges he bought wine, oil and meat for the feast. The guests knew about the switch and that evening sang before the groom "ha laya, ha laya". In Aramaic this sounds both like praise ("it is fitting, it is fitting") and like "she is Leah, she is Leah", but the groom heard only praise. The bride was brought in once the lamps had been covered. All night Jacob called her Rachel, and she answered.

"In the morning, behold, it was Leah" (Genesis 29:25). To the question "wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?" Laban has an answer ready, and it is the answer of the Hierophant in shadow: "It must not be so done in our country, to give the younger before the firstborn" (Genesis 29:26). The agreement of two people is cancelled by the custom of the place. Arguing is useless: the rule is older than the agreement, and the one who keeps the rule is the one who judges it. Wen describes the upright Hierophant as a person who "relies on another, a figure of authority or an institution, to define for the Seeker what is right and wrong". Laban is exactly such an institution in one person.

Then come seven more years of service for the woman he had served the first seven for, and after that six years for the flocks. "Your father hath deceived me, and changed my wages ten times" (Genesis 31:7). This is the middle of the tail lived in its minus: life in someone else's house, where the rules change on the way and the last word always belongs to the elders. Among the tasks of the fifth energy in a couple, Lisovskaya names living with the parents or on their support, relatives interfering even in the choice of partner, and conflict with the partner's family. Genesis has all of it at once: the son-in-law lives with his father-in-law, works for his father-in-law, and his wife is chosen by his father-in-law.

In the end Jacob has two wives, and the pain of unloved Leah in Genesis is real. But what matters for the couple's tail is not a third person; it is what replaced the one who was chosen. In a modern couple, what gets brought in on the morning after the wedding is not another person but an order of things: who comes first, what is proper, the parents' plans for the young couple. The flat where the young couple will "stay with us for now". The holiday table where everything was decided long before this couple existed. Financial help whose terms are a little different every year: the very wages changed ten times.

The numbers show why the middle feels different to each of the two. In 40% of couples with this tail, one partner has The Hierophant in the centre of their personal chart, the comfort zone. For that partner, established order is home; for the other, it is a foreign order they have come to serve. This is neither guilt nor merit, just a difference in temperature: one is at home, the other is a guest. And in 16% of couples the partners carry in the middles of their personal tails exactly the two ends of the couple's tail: one has Justice there, the other The Devil. Their sum gives The Hierophant. 15 + 8 = 23 → 5: this couple's established order is made of desire plus justice.

sections.h2: Third clue: gods under the camel's saddle
paragraphs: Jacob leaves in secret while Laban is away shearing his sheep. Two sentences side by side in Genesis read like a clue about a couple: "Rachel had stolen the images that were her father's", and Jacob, in the Hebrew, "stole the heart of Laban the Aramean", because he did not tell him he was fleeing (Genesis 31:19–20; the King James Version smooths the second into "stole away unawares"). In the Hebrew text the verb is the same, ganav, to steal. Both of them steal, each in his or her own way, and neither knows about the other's theft.

The images are the teraphim, the household gods of the father's house. Wen writes of The Devil: "The theme of The Devil is the worship of false idols." The text does not say why Rachel took them. In 1940 the Assyriologist Cyrus Gordon linked the theft to the tablets from Nuzi, where household gods went together with the right of inheritance; the hypothesis was later disputed, for example by Moshe Greenberg in 1962. But the daughters' grievance is in the text even without the tablets: "Is there yet any portion or inheritance for us in our father's house? Are we not counted of him strangers? for he hath sold us, and hath quite devoured also our money" (Genesis 31:14–15). Perhaps Rachel took her share herself, in secret, since no one intended to give it to her. That too is a court, only without witnesses.

Laban catches up with the fugitives and asks a question there is no escaping: "wherefore hast thou stolen my gods?" Jacob, sure of his own people, answers with a sentence: "With whomsoever thou findest thy gods, let him not live" (Genesis 31:32). And the text adds at once: "For Jacob knew not that Rachel had stolen them." Rachel hides the idols under the camel's saddle and sits on them: "Let it not displease my lord that I cannot rise up before thee" (Genesis 31:35). The search finds nothing.

The commentators remembered this sentence. Rashi, following the midrash, wrote: "In consequence of this curse Rachel died on the journey." A verdict passed in the heat of the moment and blind strikes the person closest. Waite's reversed Justice includes "excessive severity", and this is what it means: justice that hurries ahead before the tent has been searched.

For a 15-5-8 couple this may be the main secret of the middle of the tail. Each partner carries little gods out of the parental home: how money should be spent, who apologises first, whose holiday matters most, what is shameful and what is sacred. They are not put on the table; they travel under the saddle, and someone sits on them when anyone looks into the tent. The other partner does not know about them and so judges too confidently: "nothing like that exists here, and it never could."

sections.h2: Fourth clue: a court with no judge
paragraphs: On Mount Gilead there is no third party to sort things out. There are only the two of them and the relatives on both sides. "Set it here before my brethren and thy brethren, that they may judge betwixt us both" (Genesis 31:37). And Jacob delivers a speech that could be called a family audit: "This twenty years have I been with thee… That which was torn of beasts I brought not unto thee; I bare the loss of it… in the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night; and my sleep departed from mine eyes. Thus have I been twenty years in thy house" (Genesis 31:38–41).

The audit is honest, and that is the strength of Justice: Waite's list for the card begins "Equity, rightness, probity". But it is also twenty years of silent bookkeeping presented in a single evening. Among the tasks of the eighth energy in a couple, Lisovskaya names debts and arrears, over-responsibility that slides into control and pressure, and the ability to admit one's own fault instead of blaming everyone else. Jacob counts his losses precisely, down to the last sheep torn by beasts. His own share in the story he does not count.

The midrash says what Genesis leaves unsaid. On the morning after the wedding Jacob throws at Leah: "Deceiver, daughter of a deceiver! Did I not call thee Rachel all night, and thou didst answer me?" Leah replies: "Is there a master without apprentices? Did not thy father call thee 'Esau', and thou didst answer him?" (our translation). Shortly before he fled to Laban, Jacob himself had passed for his brother before his blind father and taken a blessing that was not his. Wen explains Justice with Newton's third law: "to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction". A deception in the dark came back to Jacob as a deception in the dark.

Laban answers the audit, and in his words the Devil of the entry speaks in the Hierophant's voice: "These daughters are my daughters, and these children are my children, and these cattle are my cattle, and all that thou seest is mine" (Genesis 31:43). But right here the story turns. Laban does not demand a trial; he proposes something else: "let us make a covenant, I and thou" (Genesis 31:44). For Wen, Justice is a balance set by people rather than by heaven, and on Mount Gilead it is set by two.

A couple recognises this easily. For years the two keep silent accounts, each their own: how much money, how many concessions, how many weekends with the other's family. Then comes the evening when the account is read out in full, like an indictment, and it turns out that the other partner has a ledger too. The main task of the tail is not to win that trial. It is to keep the account from piling up for twenty years.

sections.h2: The morning when "it was Leah": The Tower in the couple's centre
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the atmosphere between the two, what is inside and not on show. In couples with the tail 15-5-8 it is almost always the same: in 82.9% it is The Tower (16), in the remaining 17.1% The Chariot (7).

The Tower here is built in two ways, and both speak about the tail. In 40% of couples it is The Hierophant in one partner's centre and Strength in the other's: 5 + 11 = 16. And in 38% of couples both partners have Justice in the centre of their personal charts: 8 + 8 = 16. **Two pairs of scales in one house make a Tower.** Each partner carries an exact measure of what is right, and each measure is right in its own way until it collides with the other.

Waite's divinatory list for The Tower contains the word "deception", and above all it is a card of the unforeseen. For the tail 15-5-8, The Tower is that very morning when "behold, it was Leah": the truth comes out all at once and the imagined picture collapses. Lisovskaya sees both sides of such an atmosphere. In the minus: barbs, irritation and threats to leave. In the plus: support in which trials are faced hand in hand, and calm in the face of unexpected trouble. This atmosphere does not promise disasters. It promises that whatever is secret in this couple will not stay secret for long.

The Chariot in the centre gives the same story a different character: a couple that solves things by moving. Lisovskaya describes the atmosphere of The Chariot as constant motion, in which decisions are made together and both rush to defend those close to them. In Genesis it is the night when Jacob sets his children and wives on camels and crosses the river, because he is afraid his father-in-law will take his daughters back.

sections.h2: Waite's cards: two in chains, two on their knees, two on the scales
paragraphs: In the deck of Waite and Pamela Colman Smith, the tail's cards show a pair of people who change position from card to card and on the third card disappear. On The Devil a man and a woman are bound to a ring in front of the altar: "There is a ring in front of the altar, from which two chains are carried to the necks of two figures, male and female." They have tails, but, as Waite writes, "there is human intelligence in the faces, and he who is exalted above them is not to be their master for ever." Waite himself links this card to The Hierophant: the Devil's raised hand is, in his words, "the reverse of that benediction which is given by the Hierophant in the fifth card".

On The Hierophant the two are below again: "two priestly ministers in albs kneel before him", with the crossed keys at his feet. There are no chains, but a third figure still stands above the two, and he decides. Waite's divinatory list for this card opens with "Marriage, alliance", and the middle of the tail 15-5-8 rests on those words.

On Justice the two are gone altogether. A single figure sits between pillars, holding a sword and scales. Nobody stands above people any more, because there are no people left on the card, only two pans. In our reading this is the path of the tail: two people, first held in chains by a third and then blessed by a third, become the two pans of the scales. The figure in the middle is no longer a master or a priest but the agreement they have made themselves.

Waite separates this justice from a higher one: the moral law "deals unto every man according to his works", while gifts and election are not handed out by merit. Camões has a line about exactly that gap. When Jacob was given Leah instead of Rachel, he began to serve another seven years "as though he had not earned her" (our translation). Love is not a salary; it can be neither earned nor underpaid. The account of Justice covers contributions, obligations and debts, the things that can be placed on a pan. The person is never placed on the pan.

sections.h2: The heap with two names: the strong version of the tail
paragraphs: The covenant on Mount Gilead is sealed by three things, and each is a hint for a 15-5-8 couple. First a stone set up as a pillar, and a heap piled by the hands of relatives from both sides. Then a shared meal: "they did eat there upon the heap" (Genesis 31:46). And then the heap is named, and it has two names. "And Laban called it Jegar-sahadutha: but Jacob called it Galeed" (Genesis 31:47). Laban speaks Aramaic, Jacob Hebrew, and both names mean the same thing: "heap of witness".

This answers the riddle of the entry. For Lisovskaya, the point at which a couple enters the task is their "common language". At the start of the tail, the common language of the two was the language of price: years, sacrifices, IOUs. At the end, nobody needs to speak the same dialect. What is needed is for two words to mean the same thing. One partner's family may call this agreement "letting the young ones live by their own lights", the other's "not interfering", and the two themselves "our rules". The words are different; the heap is one.

The border in this covenant is drawn not by flight but by words: neither I to thee nor thou to me, "for harm". Laban writes in his own condition: not to mistreat his daughters. The parents' care stops being control and becomes a clause in the agreement. And the last verse of the chapter sounds like the resolution of the whole middle of the tail: "And early in the morning Laban rose up, and kissed his sons and his daughters, and blessed them: and Laban departed, and returned unto his place" (Genesis 31:55). The Hierophant's blessing finally stands in its proper place: after the agreement, not instead of it. And the parent goes back home.
What changes the script for a couple with this tail:

ul: **Name the price aloud while it is still small.** A move, a wait, a job given up: these are contributions to be agreed on, not IOUs to be kept. A beloved person is not "earned", and love is not bought with gifts.

**Take the gods out from under the saddle.** Each partner names the rules of the parental home they carry with them, and the two decide together which to bring into their own home and which to leave where they came from.
**Start the couple's own holidays and rules.** Get along with the family without letting it inside the couple's borders, and agree in advance where advice and help end.

**Check the account regularly, not once every twenty years.** Calmly, without a speech for the prosecution: who put in what, what is hard, what needs dividing again. And in that conversation count one's own share too, not only the other's.

**No verdict before the tent has been searched, and no searches.** Asking aloud is better than looking under the saddle. And it is not by chance that Lisovskaya lists forgiveness among the tasks of the eighth energy.

paragraphs: If there are threats, violence or fear for one's safety in a couple, this is not a matter for reading cards. What is needed then is help: a local emergency number, a crisis line, a psychologist.

The Victorian lovers engraving Mizpah on their brooches were not wrong after all. The treaty of two distrustful men became a word given before parting, because an honest border is itself a form of faithfulness. A 15-5-8 couple walks this whole path: from a bargain made for love to an agreement the two can sign together.

sections.h2: The couple's values: the road to a land of one's own
paragraphs: The couple's values are the spiritual purpose, one more answer to the question of why the two met. Couples with the tail 15-5-8 have three possible values. In 54.2% it is The World (21). Waite's divinatory list for The World includes "recompense, voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place". That is almost word for word the end of Jacob's story with Laban: "Return unto the land of thy fathers, and to thy kindred" (Genesis 31:3). The value of such a couple is a land of its own, where nobody changes the wages any more.

In 32% of couples the values card is The Hanged Man (12): Waite's list for it begins with "wisdom, circumspection, discernment", that is, the ability to wait without losing one's head, which Jacob learned over fourteen years. In 13.8% it is The Empress (3), for Waite "fruitfulness": the multiplied flocks Jacob led out of Laban's house. This is our reading, not a statement from the books, but all three converge on one thing: this couple's path leads out of someone else's house into its own.

intro: A father-in-law said them to his son-in-law. Laban said them to Jacob on Mount Gilead, after a seven-day pursuit and a search of the tents. Two men who had lived side by side for twenty years and did not trust each other piled up a heap of stones and swore "that I will not pass over this heap to thee, and that thou shalt not pass over this heap… unto me, for harm" (Genesis 31:52). The tenderest words of parted lovers were born as a border treaty. The whole story of Jacob and Rachel, from the well to that heap, is the couple's karmic tail 15-5-8.

**The tail in brief.** The union begins with a desire that both are willing to pay for, passes through someone else's house and someone else's rules, and arrives at the main task: an honest reckoning and an agreement that carries both signatures. The three cards in order:

ul: **15, The Devil — Entry to the task.** A strong "I want to be with you, whatever it costs". The strength of this entry and its hook are the same thing: the beloved easily becomes a reward that has been earned, and the years of waiting become a debt that someone has to repay.

**5, The Hierophant — Middle of the task.** The path runs through established order: the wedding, the parents, "this is how we do things", the rules of the parental homes that each partner brings along. Here the agreement of the two is constantly rewritten by a third party, whether custom or family.

**8, Justice — Main task.** To settle the account honestly: to say aloud who put in what and who owes what, to own one's share and not only the other's, and to draw the border with the parental homes by agreement rather than by flight.

intro: This is not a prediction and not a verdict. The couple's tail shows where the two of them are most likely to stumble and what they can learn together. What follows is the evidence: what is written in the cards themselves, in the books of Waite, Wen and Lisovskaya, and in the numbers shared by every couple with this tail.

faq.q: Is the karmic tail 15-5-8 in compatibility a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict events and does not pass a verdict on the union. It shows a task: a desire the two pay for, a middle where established order and family press on the couple, and a main lesson in honest reckoning and agreement. Lisovskaya reads a couple's main task mostly through its difficulties, so the description sounds stern, but the same task, solved together, becomes a support for the union.

faq.q: How is the couple's tail 15-5-8 different from the personal tail 15-5-8?
faq.a: They are different calculations. A personal tail is calculated from a single date of birth, and its points mean something else. A couple's tail is added up from the points of two personal matrices, and its roles belong to the couple: the entry to the task, the middle of the task, the couple's main task. A personal tail 15-5-8 in one partner never produces a couple tail 15-5-8: the entry of the couple's tail has to add up to exactly 15, and for that each partner needs a number below fifteen at their own entry.

faq.q: Can a couple have the tail 5-8-15 or 8-15-5?
faq.a: No. The first number of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, and of the three numbers 15, 5 and 8 only 15 is. So these cards stand in a couple's tail in only one order: The Devil at the entry, The Hierophant in the middle, Justice as the main task.

faq.q: Does the Hierophant in the middle mean the couple has to get officially married?
faq.a: No. The Hierophant describes a path through established order (marriage, families, traditions, shared rules), not an obligation to go through a ceremony. The question in the middle of this tail is not "are we registered" but "whose rules live in our home, and who chose them". A couple can live by its own rules with a marriage certificate or without one.

faq.q: Why do couples with this tail almost always have The Tower in the centre?
faq.a: That is how the numbers add up: in 38% of couples both partners have Justice in the centre of their personal charts (8 + 8 = 16), in 40% one has The Hierophant and the other Strength (5 + 11 = 16). In all, The Tower stands in the centre for 82.9% of such couples and The Chariot for 17.1%. The Tower in a couple's atmosphere does not promise misfortune: it says that what is hidden here comes out quickly and that the couple goes through such moments together.

faq.q: How can a couple find out whether its tail is 15-5-8?
faq.a: Calculate both personal matrices and add the matching points of the tail: entry to entry, middle to middle, main task to main task, reducing sums above 22. The easier way is to enter both dates of birth into the compatibility calculator: it shows the couple's tail, the centre and the couple's values at once.

report: In nineteenth-century England, lovers about to part gave each other brooches bearing the word Mizpah and a verse from Genesis: "The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another." The first to speak these words was not a lover but a father-in-law addressing his son-in-law. Laban said them to Jacob on Mount Gilead, after a pursuit and a search of the tents, when two men who had distrusted each other for twenty years piled up a heap of stones and swore not to cross it "for harm". The tenderest words of parted lovers were born as a border treaty. The tail 15-5-8 is the whole road that leads to such a heap.

The union begins with The Devil: a desire that both are willing to pay for. The middle is The Hierophant: someone else's house, established order, family and "this is how we do things". The main task is Justice: **to settle the account honestly and make an agreement that carries both signatures.**

In a couple with this tail, neither partner has The Devil at the entry of their personal tail. It appears only between them. In Jacob's story, read through the cards, this is visible from the first scene. Jacob on his own is a man of service and waiting. Rachel on her own is a beauty, the shepherdess of her father's flocks. Nothing dark. But the moment they meet, a bargain appears: "I will serve thee seven years for Rachel." The seven years "seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her."

In the sixteenth century Camões wrote a sonnet about this that names the hook more precisely than any commentary: Jacob served "not the father, he served her, and her alone he sought as his reward". Reward: this is where the Devil hides inside love. The term runs out, and Jacob says: "Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled." That is how people speak of wages.

A couple with this tail recognises itself not in passion but in the bookkeeping of passion. "I moved cities for us." "I waited three years for a decision." The desire is real, and so is the price. But **a price paid in silence turns into an IOU**, and one day it is presented for payment. Lisovskaya sums up the fifteenth energy in a couple in one thought: nobody belongs to anybody.

report.h3: The rule is older than the agreement

report: Jacob gets his wedding by all the rules, with a feast for all the men of the place. The midrash adds a detail: the guests knew about the switch and sang "ha laya" to the groom, which sounds both like praise and like "she is Leah". In the morning, behold, it was Leah. To the question "wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?" Laban has the Hierophant's answer in shadow ready: "It must not be so done in our country, to give the younger before the firstborn." The agreement of two people is cancelled by the custom of the place. Then come seven more years of service, and a father-in-law who "changed my wages ten times".

In a modern couple, what gets brought in on the morning after the wedding is not another person but an order of things: "stay with us for now", a holiday table where everything was decided long before this couple existed, financial help whose terms are a little different every year. The agreement of the two is constantly rewritten by a third party.

report.h3: Gods under the saddle and a blind verdict

report: When Jacob leaves in secret, Genesis puts two sentences side by side: Rachel stole her father's idols, and Jacob "stole the heart of Laban" by not telling him he was going. In the Hebrew text the verb is the same. Both of them steal, and neither knows about the other's theft. Laban catches up and asks about his gods. Jacob, sure of his own people, passes sentence: "With whomsoever thou findest thy gods, let him not live." And the text adds: "For Jacob knew not that Rachel had stolen them." She is sitting on the idols, hidden under the camel's saddle.

This is the main secret of the middle of the tail. Each partner carries little gods out of the parental home: how money should be spent, who apologises first, whose holiday matters most. They are not put on the table; they travel under the saddle. And the other partner, not knowing about them, **judges too confidently and strikes the person closest.**

On Mount Gilead there is no judge, only the two of them and the relatives on both sides. Jacob delivers a family audit: "This twenty years have I been with thee… That which was torn of beasts I brought not unto thee; I bare the loss of it… Thus have I been twenty years in thy house." The audit is honest, but it is also twenty years of accounts presented in a single evening. His own share Jacob does not count. The midrash keeps the reply Jacob heard from Leah on the morning after the wedding, when he accused her of deceit: "Is there a master without apprentices? Did not thy father call thee 'Esau', and thou didst answer him?" A deception in the dark came back to him as a deception in the dark.
The main task of the tail is not to win that trial. It is to keep the account from piling up for twenty years.

Laban answers: "all that thou seest is mine", and at once proposes not a trial but a covenant. The heap receives two names: Laban names it in Aramaic, Jacob in Hebrew, and both mean "heap of witness". Two families do not need to speak one language; they need their words to mean the same thing. In the morning Laban blesses his daughters and grandchildren, and the text says that he "returned unto his place". **The blessing comes after the agreement, not instead of it.**

What changes the script: naming the price aloud while it is still small; taking the gods out from under the saddle and deciding together which rules of the parental homes to bring into a home of one's own; starting the couple's own holidays and agreeing in advance where the family's advice and help end; checking the account regularly, counting one's own share too; passing no verdict before the tent has been searched.

If there are threats, violence or fear for one's safety in a couple, this is not a matter for reading cards: what is needed is help, from a local emergency number or crisis line, or from a psychologist.

The lovers with their Mizpah brooches were not wrong. The treaty of two distrustful men became a word of faithfulness, because an honest border is itself a form of it. A 15-5-8 couple walks this whole road: from a bargain made for love to an agreement the two can sign together.
